claim: Four homologous bacterial allosteric transcription factors (TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR) were studied using deep mutational scanning.
source: We carried out deep mutational scanning (DMS) of four homologous bacterial allosteric transcription factors (aTFs) to identify hotspots
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that DMS was performed on four homologous bacterial aTFs.

claim: Allosteric hotspots are distributed protein-wide rather than being restricted to pathways linking allosteric and active sites.
source: We found hotspots to be distributed protein-wide rather than being restricted to 'pathways' linking allosteric and active sites as is commonly assumed.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from the DMS analysis.

claim: The location of allosteric hotspots is not superimposable across the four aTF homologs despite structural homology.
source: Despite structural homology, the location of hotspots was not superimposable across the aTFs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this observation from comparing the four aTFs.

claim: Common signatures emerge when comparing hotspots coincident with long-range interactions, suggesting conserved allosteric mechanism among homologs.
source: However, common signatures emerged when comparing hotspots coincident with long-range interactions, suggesting that the allosteric mechanism is conserved among the homologs despite differences in molecular details.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from analyzing long-range interactions.

claim: Global structural and dynamic properties are stronger predictors of allosteric hotspots than local and physicochemical properties.
source: Machine learning with our large DMS datasets revealed global structural and dynamic properties to be a strong predictor of whether a residue is a hotspot than local and physicochemical properties.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from machine learning analysis.

claim: A machine learning model trained on one protein can predict hotspots in a homologous protein.
source: Furthermore, a model trained on one protein can predict hotspots in a homolog.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this capability of the machine learning model.

claim: The overall allosteric mechanism is embedded in the structural fold of the aTF family, but molecular details are sequence-specific.
source: In summary, the overall allosteric mechanism is embedded in the structural fold of the aTF family, but the finer, molecular details are sequence-specific.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion from the study.

claim: All allosteric proteins obey a thermodynamic principle where binding an effector ligand stabilizes the active state over the inactive state.
source: Though allosteric proteins may employ diverse structural mechanisms to propagate the perturbation, all allosteric proteins obey a simple thermodynamic principle that binding an effector ligand stabilizes the active state over the inactive state and removing the effector ligand reverses this effect (Changeux, 2012; Cui and Karplus, 2008; Marzen et al., 2013; Hilser et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction states this principle with supporting citations.

claim: Deep mutational scanning of TetR revealed that allosteric hotspots are distributed throughout the protein with no apparent direct structural link to either the allosteric or active site.
source: Our recent deep mutational scanning (DMS) analysis of bacterial transcription factor, TetR, revealed that allosteric hotspots are distributed throughout the protein with no apparent direct structural link to either the allosteric or the active site (Leander et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous DMS study on TetR.

claim: The commonly held view is that hotspot residues tend to fall along well-defined pathways linking allosteric and active sites.
source: In contrast, the commonly held view is that hotspot residues tend to fall along well-defined pathways linking both sites (Ota and Agard, 2005; Süel et al., 2003; Strickland et al., 2008; Reynolds et al., 2011; Amor et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction states this as a commonly held view with supporting citations.

claim: The TetR family of proteins share a similar protein structure despite their diversity.
source: Despite their diversity, all TetR family proteins (>100 in PDB) share a similar protein structure which suggests their structure is versatile and robust to preserve allostery while accommodating diverse sequences (Cuthbertson and Nodwell, 2013; Fukami-Kobayashi et al., 2003).
evidence: The results section states this observation about TetR family proteins with citations.

claim: The four aTFs studied (TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR) have high structural similarity (between 1 and 3 Å Cα RMSD) but low sequence identity (between 14% and 19%).
source: We chose four aTFs – TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR – with high structural similarity (between 1 and 3 Å Cα root mean squared distance [RMSD]) but low sequence identity (between 14% and 19%, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states these structural and sequence properties.

claim: Wild-type TetR has a fold induction of 49-fold with anhydrotetracycline as ligand.
source: Fold induction of wild-type aTFs was TetR: 49-fold (ligand: anhydrotetracycline [aTC])
evidence: The results section explicitly states this experimental measurement.

claim: Wild-type TtgR has a fold induction of 25-fold with naringenin as ligand.
source: TtgR: 25-fold (ligand: naringenin [Nar])
evidence: The results section explicitly states this experimental measurement.

claim: Wild-type MphR has a fold induction of 100-fold with erythromycin as ligand.
source: MphR: 100-fold (ligand: erythromycin [Ery])
evidence: The results section explicitly states this experimental measurement.

claim: Wild-type RolR has a fold induction of 15-fold with resorcinol as ligand.
source: RolR: 15-fold (ligand: resorcinol [Res])
evidence: The results section explicitly states this experimental measurement.

claim: Comprehensive libraries of point mutants were created with approximately 3800 mutants per aTF (~200 residues × 19 mutants/residue).
source: We mutated each aTF using commercially available chip oligonucleotides to encode a comprehensive library of point mutants by single-site saturation mutagenesis of each residue (~200 residues per aTF × 19 mutants/residue = 3800 mutants per aTF, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly describes the library construction.

claim: Dead variants are well-folded proteins that bind to DNA and repress transcription but cannot be induced with the ligand.
source: The dead variants are well-folded proteins that bind to DNA and repress transcription but cannot be induced with the ligand.
evidence: The results section explicitly defines the properties of dead variants.

claim: 53, 51, 48, and 57 residues were designated as hotspots in TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR, respectively.
source: We designated 53, 51, 48, and 57 residues as hotspots in TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR, respectively.
evidence: The results section explicitly states the number of hotspots identified.

claim: After excluding ligand-contacting residues, 41, 43, 29, and 51 hotspots remained in TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR, respectively.
source: After excluding ligand-contacting residues from consideration, as mutations at these residues appeared dead likely due to loss of ligand affinity, we were left with 41, 43, 29, and 51 hotspots in TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR, respectively.
evidence: The results section explicitly states these numbers after filtering.

claim: Hotspots of TetR and MphR were concentrated in the C-terminal half of the protein.
source: Hotspots of TetR and MphR were concentrated in the C-terminal half of the protein (Figure 1B)
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Hotspots of TtgR and RolR were distributed across the entire structure.
source: whereas those of TtgR and RolR were distributed across the entire structure.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation.

claim: A high fraction of hotspots, relative to segment length, were at the dimer interface.
source: First, a high fraction of hotspots, relative to the segment's length, were at the dimer interface (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: A high fraction of hotspots was on α4, suggesting it acts as a mechanical link transmitting allosteric signals from the LBD to the DBD.
source: Second, a high fraction of hotspots was on α4 suggesting α4 acts as a mechanical link that transmits allosteric signals from the LBD to the DBD.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation and interpretation.

claim: Very few hotspots were in the DBD compared to other regions.
source: Third, very few hotspots were in the DBD compared to other regions.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation.

claim: Allosteric hotspots are not statistically more conserved than non-hotspots when compared to close sequence homologs (>50% sequence identity).
source: We compared hotspots to close sequence homologs (>50% sequence identity) and did not find statistically higher sequence conservation in hotspots over non-hotspots (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The overlap between Ohm webserver predictions and experimental hotspots is modest and involves mostly DBD residues.
source: The overlap between predictions and experiments is modest and involves mostly DBD residues while the experimental hotspots are distributed across the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this comparison with reference to a figure.

claim: Long-range interactions (LRIs) were defined as residues separated by 10 or more positions in sequence but within 8 Å in Cα-Cα distance.
source: We generated contact maps of residue-residue interactions and selected LRIs as residues separated by 10 or more positions in sequence but within 8 Å in Cα- Cα distance.
evidence: The results section explicitly defines the criteria for LRIs.

claim: In all four aTFs, hotspots constituted a higher fraction of LRIs than non-hotspots (p=0.07).
source: In all four aTFs, hotspots constituted a higher fraction of LRIs than non-hotspots (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; p=0.07).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this statistical finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Hotspots in TetR and MphR are especially enriched in LRIs – 28% hotspots vs. 17% non-hotspots.
source: Hotspots in TetR and MphR are especially enriched in LRIs – 28% hotspots vs. 17% non-hotspots.
evidence: The results section explicitly states these percentages.

claim: The gap in LRI enrichment is smaller in TtgR and RolR – 23% hotspots and 20% non-hotspots.
source: This gap is smaller in TtgR and RolR – 23% hotspots and 20% non-hotspots.
evidence: The results section explicitly states these percentages.

claim: The optimal number of LRI clusters for each aTF was determined to be 10 using the Elbow method.
source: The optimal number of clusters is the point yielding diminishing returns (higher variance within a cluster) that is not worth the cost of adding new clusters and was found to be 10 clusters independently for each aTF (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The dimer interface emerged as the first-ranked LRI cluster in TetR, MphR, and RolR.
source: The dimer interface emerged as the first-ranked cluster in TetR, MphR, and RolR (Figure 2B)
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The first-ranked LRI cluster of TtgR was not the dimer interface, consistent with far fewer hotspots found at the dimer interface of TtgR.
source: The first-ranked cluster of TtgR was not the dimer interface which is consistent with far fewer hotspots found at the dimer interface of TtgR (Figures 2 and 1C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation with reference to figures.

claim: Aromatic amino acids (Phe, Trp, and Tyr) were enriched among dead variants (20%) over the not-dead group (15%).
source: Aromatic amino acids (Phe, Trp, and Tyr) were enriched among dead variants (20%) over the not-dead group (15%) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Mutations to proline were enriched among dead variants (5%) vs. the not-dead group (3.8%).
source: Mutations to proline were also enriched, albeit to a lesser degree, among the dead variants (5%) vs. the not-dead group (3.8%).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Statistically significant differences were observed in polarizability, SASA, and mass between dead and not-dead variants.
source: However, we observed statistically significant differences in polarizability, solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), and mass (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: No statistically significant differences were observed in hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, and polarity between dead and not-dead variants.
source: We did not observe any statistically significant differences in hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, and polarity between both groups (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Aromatic amino acids (Trp, Phe, Tyr) and strongly aliphatic amino acids (Ile and Leu) have the highest interaction energies among all amino acids in the PDB (−4 to –6 RT units).
source: These amino acids (Trp, Phe, Tyr, Ile, and Leu) have the highest interaction energies among all amino acids in the PDB of (−4 to –6 RT units) (Chan et al., 2004).
evidence: The results section states this with a citation.

claim: Mutations to small branched amino acids (Ser, Cys, and Ala) were most depleted among dead variants (12%) vs. the not-dead group (18%).
source: At the other end, mutations to small branched amino acids (Ser, Cys, and Ala), which have low interaction energies, were most depleted among dead variants (12%) vs. the not-dead group (18%)
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: In the inactive C144F TetR variant, F144 formed strong aromatic interactions at the dimer interface with F140 and H139 in the other monomer.
source: In the inactive C144F TetR variant, F144 formed strong aromatic interactions at the dimer interface with its neighbor F140 and H139 in the other monomer, potentially stabilizing the inactive state of the protein through increased dimerization interactions (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section explicitly describes this structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: 27 features potentially relevant to the classification of a protein site as an allosteric hotspot were assembled.
source: Accordingly, we assembled a comprehensive list of 27 features that are potentially relevant to the classification of a protein site as an allosteric hotspot (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this with reference to a figure.

claim: The 27 features include eight intrinsic physicochemical properties of amino acids, eight local structural properties, and 11 global features.
source: These include eight intrinsic physicochemical properties of amino acids such as charge and hydrophobicity, and eight local structural properties, such as solvent accessibility, local structural entropy (LSE) (Jenik et al., 2012), and frustration index (Chakrabarty and Parekh, 2016). Since allostery is fundamentally about cooperativity between distant sites in a protein, we also included 11 global features that describe long-range structural or dynamical properties
evidence: The results section explicitly describes the feature categories.

claim: For all four aTFs, global features have the highest F scores and physicochemical features tend to have the lowest F scores.
source: For all four aTFs, global features have the highest F scores and physicochemical features tend to have the lowest F scores.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The F1 scores of the best model and that of a random model are: 0.83 and 0.19 for TetR, 0.82 and 0.16 for MphR, 0.64 and 0.26 for RolR, and 0.54 and 0.21 for TtgR.
source: The F1 scores of the best model and that of a random model for each protein are: 0.83 and 0.19 for TetR, 0.82 and 0.16 for MphR, 0.64 and 0.26 for RolR, and 0.54 and 0.21 for TtgR
evidence: The results section explicitly states these performance metrics.

claim: All best models significantly outperform their corresponding random models.
source: The results illustrate that all best models significantly outperform their corresponding random models, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining subsets of the 27 features in describing hotspots.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: RolR and TtgR exhibit significant numbers of false positive hotspots predicted by the GA-NN models.
source: However, the performances of the models are not uniform across the four proteins, with RolR and TtgR exhibiting significant numbers of false positive hotspots predicted by the GA-NN models (blue regions in Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The five most frequent features in the optimal models of the four proteins consist of 71.4% global features, 14.8% local features, and 14.8% physicochemical properties.
source: Nevertheless, the five most frequent features in the optimal models of the four proteins consist of 71.4% global features, 14.8% local features, and 14.8% physicochemical properties of wild-type amino acids
evidence: The results section explicitly states this breakdown.

claim: Distances to centrality peaks are among the most frequent global features for all four aTFs.
source: For example, distances to centrality peaks are among the most frequent global features for all four aTFs
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation.

claim: CPP_TL significantly outperforms CPP as well as models trained with 10% data for the test protein only.
source: CPP_TL significantly outperforms their CPP counterparts as well as the corresponding best models trained with 10% data for the test protein only (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: NNs trained with data of three proteins generally outperform NNs trained with data of only one protein in predicting on the fourth protein.
source: It's also noted that NNs trained with data of three proteins in general outperform NNs trained with the data of only one of them in predicting on the fourth protein (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation with reference to a figure.

claim: All relative performances of transfer learning with homology models are above 83%.
source: Nevertheless, all relative performances are above 83%, which is remarkable considering that the lowest sequence identity between a modeled protein and its template is only 15.4% (Supplementary file 4)
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: There is a general trend of increasing model performance with increasing sequence similarity between template protein and target protein.
source: We observed a general trend of increasing model performance with increasing sequence similarity between template protein and MphR
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation.

claim: There is a general trend of decreasing model performance with increasing RMSD between template protein and target protein.
source: and decreasing model performance with increasing RMSD between template protein and MphR (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation with reference to figures.

claim: UniRep feature-based models perform significantly better than random baselines in both mutation phenotype prediction and hotspot prediction for all four homologous aTFs.
source: As summarized in Tables 1–2, UniRep feature-based models perform significantly better than the random baselines in both mutation phenotype prediction and hotspot prediction for all four homologous aTFs
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to tables.

claim: There is a noticeable gap between hotspot prediction performance using UniRep features and optimal models using the 27 physical features.
source: However, there is a noticeable gap between hotspot prediction performance using UniRep features and our optimal models.
evidence: The results section explicitly states this observation.

claim: When 1900 UniRep features are combined with the 27 physical features, a marginal yet consistent improvement in mutation phenotype prediction is observed.
source: When the 1900 UniRep features are combined with the 27 physical features in our model, a marginal yet consistent improvement in mutation phenotype prediction is observed (Table 1).
evidence: The results section explicitly states this finding with reference to a table.

claim: Hotspot residues are distributed across the structure rather than being limited to specific pathways connecting inducer and DNA-binding sites.
source: First, hotspot residues are distributed across the structure rather than being limited to the specific pathway(s) that connect the inducer and DNA-binding sites as commonly assumed in allostery models.
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this finding.

claim: Hotspots are relatively enriched near the dimerization interface and α4 helix at the LBD/DBD interface.
source: Nonetheless, they are relatively enriched near the dimerization interface and α4 helix at the LBD/DBD interface, highlighting the role of these regions in signal transmission (Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this finding with a citation.

claim: Long-range interactions are more prevalent among hotspots, suggesting they are critical for propagating allosteric signals.
source: Second, we observe that LRIs (in terms of sequence separation) are more prevalent among hotspots, suggesting that in addition to being important to folding and stability, LRIs are also relevant to propagating allostery signals.
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this finding.

claim: A generally similar allostery mechanism is at play in the homologous proteins studied.
source: These results support the idea that a generally similar allostery mechanism is at play in these homologous proteins.
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this conclusion.

claim: Allostery mechanisms in homologous proteins may differ substantially in fine details.
source: As discussed above, these differences might suggest a higher level of complexity in the allostery mechanism in TtgR and RolR, in which the hotspot residues may contribute to both intra-domain properties and inter-domain coupling. Therefore, allostery mechanisms in homologous proteins may differ substantially in fine details
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this conclusion.

claim: The transfer learning approach can be effective for cross-protein predictions.
source: Along this line, it is satisfying to observe that the TL approach can be rather effective for CPPs
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this finding.

claim: The TL performance is not highly sensitive to the resolution of the structural model.
source: the fact that the performance is not highly sensitive to the resolution of the structural model is particularly encouraging, especially considering recent advances in protein structure predictions (Orth et al., 2000).
evidence: The concluding remarks explicitly state this observation with a citation.

claim: Comprehensive single-mutant libraries of TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR were generated by replacing all wild-type residues to all other 19 canonical amino acids starting at position 2.
source: Comprehensive single-mutant libraries of TetR, TtgR, MphR, and RolR were generated by replacing all wild-type residues to all other 19 canonical amino acids starting at position 2 (total mutant sequences – TetR: 3914; TtgR: 3971; MphR: 3667; RolR: 4332).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the library construction.

claim: A read threshold of 5 was applied across all replicates, conditions, and proteins to reduce sequencing noise.
source: A read threshold of 5 was then applied across all replicates, conditions, and proteins to reduce sequencing noise
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this threshold.

claim: Increasing the read threshold to 10 did not significantly affect final analyses or positions identified as hotspots.
source: increasing this threshold to 10 reads did not significantly affect final analyses or positions identified as hotspots (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Residues with weighted scores above the calculated Q3 were identified as allosteric hotspots.
source: The interquartile range of weighted scores for every protein was calculated and positions with weighted scores above the calculated Q3 were identified as allosteric hotspots (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes this criterion with reference to a figure.

claim: Homologs of TtgR, MphR, and RolR were identified using HMM search against UniProtKB database.
source: Homologs of TtgR, MphR, and RolR were identified using HMM search (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/hmmer/) (Larkin et al., 2007) against UniProtKB database with individual sequences used as queries.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes this procedure with a citation.

claim: Positions with a conservation score of 7 or more were termed highly conserved.
source: Conservation score in Jalview is computed by AMAS tool (Vehlow et al., 2011) and positions with a score of 7 or more were termed highly conserved.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this criterion with a citation.

claim: Contact maps of TetR homologs were generated using CMView.
source: Contact maps of TetR homologs were generated using CMView (Kellogg et al., 2011).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: Interactions between α carbon atoms within 8 Å were identified with a minimum sequence separation of 10 residues to select for LRIs.
source: Interactions between α carbon atoms within 8 Å of were identified and a minimum sequence separation of 10 residues was set to select for LRIs.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes these criteria.

claim: The elbow method was used to determine the optimal number of clusters for k-means clustering of LRIs.
source: The elbow method was used to determine the optimal number of clusters in which the within-cluster sum of squares was minimized (Figure 2—figure supplement 2); 10 clusters were chosen for each homolog.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes this method with reference to a figure.

claim: All modeling calculations were performed using the Rosetta molecular modeling suite v3.9.
source: All modeling calculations were performed using the Rosetta molecular modeling suite v3.9.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this.

claim: Single-point mutants were generated using the standard ddg_monomer application in Rosetta.
source: Single-point mutants were generated using the standard ddg_monomer application (Kawashima and Kanehisa, 2000), which enables local conformational to minimize energy.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: The eight physicochemical properties of wild-type amino acids were obtained from the AAindex database.
source: The eight physicochemical properties of wild-type amino acids, molecular weight, number of electrostatic charges, hydrophobicity, aromaticity, number of potential hydrogen bond, polarity, polarizability, and flexibility are obtained from the AAindex database (Waterhouse et al., 2018).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: Backbone entropy loss and sidechain entropy loss were calculated with the PLOPS webserver.
source: Backbone entropy loss and sidechain entropy loss of a residue, measuring the loss of conformational entropy of a residue upon protein folding, were calculated with the PLOPS webserver based on the crystal structure of the protein (Joosten et al., 2011).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: SASA was calculated with the DSSP webserver.
source: SASA was calculated with the DSSP webserver (Kabsch and Sander, 1983; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with citations.

claim: The single-residue frustration index was calculated with AWSEM-MD Frustratometer.
source: The single-residue frustration index was calculated with AWSEM-MD Frustratometer based on the crystal structure of the protein (Chakrabarty and Parekh, 2016).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: X-ray crystallographic B-factor of a residue was obtained from the ENM webserver.
source: X-ray crystallographic B-factor of a residue was obtained from the ENM webserver (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: Orientational cross-correlations between residue fluctuations are calculated using the ENM server.
source: Orientational cross-correlations between residue fluctuations are calculated using the ENM server (Li et al., 2017), the values vary from –1 (fully anticorrelated motions) to +1 (fully correlated).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: Centrality scores of each residue were calculated using the Network Analysis of Protein Structures (NAPS) server.
source: Centrality scores of each residue were calculated using the Network Analysis of Protein Structures (NAPS) server (http://bioinf.iiit.ac.in/NAPS/) (Bahar and Rader, 2005).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states this with a citation.

claim: All implemented NNs (except those involving UniRep features) have one hidden layer of 10 neurons with RELU activation and 2 neurons with softmax activation in the output layer.
source: All implemented NNs (except those involving UniRep features) have one hidden layer of 10 neurons (with RELU activation) and 2 neurons (with softmax activation) in the output layer.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly describes the NN architecture.

claim: Xavier initialization, Adams optimizer, categorical cross-entropy loss function, and a learning rate of 0.0007 were used in all NN cases.
source: Xavier initialization, Adams optimizer, categorical cross-entropy loss function, and a learning rate of 0.0007 were used in all cases.
evidence: The Materials and methods section explicitly states these hyperparameters.
